1.b3 d5 2.Bb2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, aiming at e5 and the kingside, so that ...e5 needs preparation. White controls the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. The price is that Black may build a broad pawn centre first, and White has to challenge it later.

1.b3 d5 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and covers e5 and d4, so that ...e5 stays hard to achieve even before the bishop arrives; the position is the same as after 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3. White keeps the set-up flexible and aims at a slow fight for the centre. The cost is that Black has a free hand in the centre, and many lines are rated only equal.

1.b3 d5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the diagonal of the king's bishop and keeps the pawn structure flexible, with development and a later challenge to d5 in mind. The move is sound but modest: it lets Black choose the pawn structure first.

1.b3 d5 2.c4.strategy: Attacks d5 at once, aiming for an English-style set-up with Bb2 behind it. After 2...dxc4 3.bxc4 White has the half-open b-file and an extra centre pawn but an isolated a-pawn, while 2...d4 gains space for Black. Playable, but Black chooses the structure before White has developed a piece.

1.b3 d5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares e4 for a reversed Old Indian set-up. It is flexible and sound, yet passive: Black takes the centre at once and meets e4 on equal terms.

1.b3 d5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and transposes into a Queen's Pawn Game in which b3 is already played. Sound but slow: nothing is done against d5, so Black completes development at ease.

1.b3 d5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, so that one bishop bears down on d5 and the other, from b2, on the long dark diagonal. Black develops freely or takes space in the centre, and White must find the moment to strike back there. Playable, but it leaves the centre undisputed.

1.b3 d5 2.f4.strategy: Takes control of e5 and prepares a Bird-style set-up. It weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and the e3 square and commits the f-pawn before Black has shown a set-up; sound, but it gives up the flexibility of the other moves.

1.b3 d5 2.Ba3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Graz Attack
1.b3 d5 2.Ba3.strategy: Aims the bishop at e7 and f8, so that ...e6 allows Bxf8 and forces ...Kxf8, which costs Black the right to castle. The bishop gives up the long diagonal and has little else to hit, so Black can simply develop, while 2...c5 would drop a pawn to Bxc5.

1.b3 d5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight onto c3, on the long diagonal that b3 prepared for the bishop, and 2...d4 attacks it at once, gains space and forces it to move again. White loses a tempo, and a later Bb2 bites on the pawn on d4.

1.b3 d5 2.c3.strategy: Blocks the long diagonal that b3 prepared for the bishop, since a bishop on b2 would now face its own pawn on c3. Black develops freely, and White has spent a tempo undoing the point of b3.

1.b3 d5 2.Na3.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b5, while c4 is covered by the d5 pawn. It does nothing for the centre, ...c6 also takes b5 away, and Black builds the centre at leisure.

1.b3 d5 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5, but 2...Bxh3 forces 3.gxh3, since the f1 bishop is blocked by g2, and leaves White with doubled, isolated h-pawns. Even without the exchange the knight stands badly on the rim.

1.b3 d5 2.b4.strategy: Pushes the same pawn a second time, reaching the position after 1.b4 d5 with Black to move, a full tempo down. On b4 the pawn is easy to attack, by the a-pawn, the queen or, once the e-pawn has moved, the f8 bishop, and it needs support from a3 or c3.

1.b3 d5 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but takes f3 from the g1 knight and weakens the e1-h4 diagonal. Black develops freely and White has spent a tempo without developing a piece.

1.b3 d5 2.a3.strategy: A waiting move that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre; it only takes b4 from Black's pieces. Black sets up at leisure.

1.b3 d5 2.a4.strategy: Pushes a flank pawn that neither develops a piece nor contests the centre. It controls b5 but leaves b4 weak, and Black takes the centre at leisure.

1.b3 d5 2.h3.strategy: Takes g4 from the c8 bishop but spends a tempo on a prophylactic move before any piece is developed, handing Black the centre.

1.b3 d5 2.h4.strategy: Gains space on the kingside and prepares h5, but does nothing for the centre or development and weakens the squares g3 and g4. Black simply develops.

1.b3 d5 2.e4.strategy: Puts a pawn on e4 where d5 attacks it and nothing defends it, so 2...dxe4 simply wins it. The bishop's pressure on g7 is easily parried, and Black keeps the extra pawn.

1.b3 d5 2.g4.strategy: Loses a pawn to 2...Bxg4: ...d5 has opened the c8-h3 diagonal and nothing protects g4. White gets no compensation and has also weakened the kingside.

1.b3 d5.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Classical Variation
1.b3 d5.background: Aron Nimzowitsch more often reached this kind of position through 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3, a move order that rules out ...e5. After 1.b3 itself, 1...d5 is Black's second most common reply, in about 27 percent of games.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square: it guards d5, covers e4 and blocks the long diagonal, so ...g6 and ...Bg7 become possible without dropping the h8-rook. Black commits to no pawn structure yet and keeps its pawn moves and bishop development open, while White's c4 lever against d5 stays available. Flexible and safe, at the price of letting White choose the set-up.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 c5.background: The Nimzo-Indian Defence is a popular defence to 1.d4; after 3.e3 Nc6 4.Nf3 Nf6 5.Bb5 White has it with colours reversed and an extra tempo. Aron Nimzowitsch reached that position against Rudolf Spielmann at New York 1927, by the move order 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 c5 3.Bb2 Nc6 4.e3 Nf6 5.Bb5, and won in 55 moves.
1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 before White can occupy it and builds a broad c5 and d5 pawn front, with natural development to follow. White often answers by pinning the c6-knight and fighting for e5 and d4. The cost is that d5 lacks pawn support until ...e6, and White can give up the bishop on c6 to plant a knight on e5.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bf5.background: Baadur Jobava beat Yu Yangyi from this position at the Tata Steel Challengers 2014 in Wijk aan Zee, answering with 3.e3 e6 4.h3 h6 5.Nc3 Bh7 6.d4 and castling queenside on move 9.
1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 shuts it in, aiming for a solid, compact set-up. The bishop covers e4, so White must prepare that advance slowly. Black develops easily, but the bishop can become a target.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bg4.background: Raymond Keene, later the author of the book Nimzowitsch/Larsen Attack (1977), had the position after 3.Nf3 as White against Vlatko Kovačević at Amsterdam 1973, reached there by 1.Nf3 d5 2.b3 Bg4 3.Bb2, and won after 3…Nd7 4.g3 Bxf3 5.exf3.
1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the e2-pawn against the queen, so White cannot play 3.e3 without losing the queen to ...Bxd1. Black stays ready to give up the bishop for a knight on f3 when the recapture damages White's pawns or removes a guard of e5.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, so Black can develop and castle quickly. Sound, but it shuts in the c8-bishop before …Bf5 or …Bg4 is possible, which is why Black usually develops that bishop first, while White builds freely.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5, but 3.Nf3 rules out that advance for now, since Nxe5 Nxe5 Bxe5 wins a pawn. Sound, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and lets White decide the set-up.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and keeps the c8-bishop free to develop outside the pawn chain before …e6. Sound but passive: the pawn controls neither d4 nor e5, takes c6 from the b8-knight, and a later …c5 costs a second move, so White builds freely.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 b6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up by preparing …Bb7, but on the other long diagonal, where the bishop looks at its own d5-pawn. It does little until …c5 and …d4 or an exchange opens that diagonal, while White builds freely. Sound but unambitious.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Nd7.strategy: Guards e5 and so prepares …e5. But it shuts in the c8-bishop and cuts the queen's guard of d5, and after 3.Nf3 an immediate …e5 still loses a pawn to Nxe5 and Bxe5. Playable but passive.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for d4 or e5, which it would cover from c6. White builds without opposition.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bd7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a passive square where it cuts the queen's guard of d5 and blocks the b8-knight's route to d7. Nothing is attacked, so White can pressure a d5-pawn that needs …c6 or …e6 to hold.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Be6.strategy: Blocks the e7-pawn, so neither …e6 nor …e5 can be played until the bishop moves again, and the bishop does less on e6 than on f5 or g4. White builds without obstruction.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early, where it blocks the c8-bishop and the b8-knight's route to d7. Nothing is attacked, so White gains time while the queen stands in the way.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early onto the a3–f8 diagonal, where 3.Ba3 attacks it at once, and Nc3 with Nb5 can hit it again later. No minor piece is developed, and the queen takes d6 from the f8-bishop.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Nh6.strategy: Puts the g8-knight on the rim on its way to f5, instead of on f6, where it would cover e4 and block the long diagonal. White builds without resistance.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn without developing a piece or touching the centre; its point is …b5, and meanwhile White takes space freely.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space with the idea …a4 against the b3-pawn, but develops nothing, and the a-pawn no longer covers b6. White builds unopposed.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 b5.strategy: Advances a flank pawn without developing a piece, and the pawn on b5 has no defender: 3.e3 already threatens Bxb5+, and a4 can strike at it as well.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 f6.strategy: Prepares …e5 and blocks the long diagonal, but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal without developing a piece. White builds a centre at leisure.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 f5.strategy: Commits at once to a Stonewall-style pawn formation that leaves e5 as a lasting hole for Bb2 and a knight, and the f5-pawn shuts the c8-bishop out of f5, g4 and h3. The e8–h5 diagonal is opened as well.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a prophylactic pawn move that prevents nothing White threatens, while White develops and claims the centre.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 h5.strategy: Starts a flank advance without developing a piece. The h-pawn weakens g5 and g6 and commits to an attack with no pieces behind it, leaving the centre to White.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 d4.strategy: Grabs space and blocks the long diagonal, but the pawn is guarded only by the queen while Bb2 already attacks it. 3.Nf3 or 3.e3 adds pressure, so Black must spend more moves to hold it, and the pawn no longer covers c4 and e4.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop at once to 3.gxh3 or 3.Nxh3, because no black piece can recapture on h3.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 Kd7.strategy: Forfeits castling for no reason and puts the king on d7, where it cuts the queen's guard of d5 and blocks the c8-bishop. The king stays exposed in the centre, and the h8-rook is out of play.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 e5.strategy: Hangs the e-pawn, because nothing guards e5 and 3.Bxe5 wins it. After 3…Nc6 the bishop simply retreats to b2, so the tempo gained is not enough and White keeps the extra pawn.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 g6.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to h8, so 3.Bxh8 wins the rook outright and nothing of Black's can recapture. The fianchetto only works once …Nf6 has blocked the diagonal.

1.b3 d5 2.Bb2 g5.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to h8, so 3.Bxh8 wins the rook for nothing, since nothing of Black's can recapture. The kingside is loosened for no gain.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, controls e4 and commits no pawn, so every set-up stays open. It also shields g7 and h8 from the long diagonal of White's coming bishop. Nothing is conceded, and the position can grow into a solid centre or a reversed Nimzo-Indian.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 from the flank and prepares to develop the knights to c6 and f6, so Black fights for the centre before White occupies it. The pawn stands on the a3–f8 diagonal, where Ba3 can attack it, so it needs support. The set-up resembles a reversed Nimzo-Indian in which White has an extra tempo.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 e5.strategy: Builds the classical d5–e5 pawn centre that White's set-up aims to undermine. The cost is that the e5-pawn comes under pressure from White's bishop on the long diagonal and later from f4, so Black must keep it firmly defended. Black takes space at once, but the centre is a target.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, in the manner of a reversed London System. Black's development is easy and solid, but the exposed bishop can be challenged, and White can prepare e4 to disturb the set-up.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the f8-bishop, but shuts in the c8-bishop before ...Bf5 is possible, giving up one of the main set-ups for no gain. Sound, yet White builds freely and keeps both c4 and d4 available.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so Black gives up the set-ups built on that pawn, and Bb5 can pin it at once. Sound, but less flexible than developing the king's knight.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a Slav-style pawn and keeps the c8-bishop free to reach f5 before ...e6. It fights for neither d4 nor e5, so White develops easily. Sound but reactive, and the pawn takes c6 from the b8-knight.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 b6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up by preparing ...Bb7. The bishop on b7 looks at its own d5-pawn, so it does little until that pawn moves or is exchanged and the diagonal opens. Sound but unambitious, and White develops freely.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7, but once White's bishop reaches b2 it attacks the h8-rook along the long diagonal, and ...Bg7 would lose the bishop to Bxg7, since nothing recaptures on g7. Black must first block the diagonal, so the long diagonal gives White the initiative. Playable, but awkward.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 but leaves a hole on e5, on the diagonal of a bishop on b2, and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal, so Qh5+ is already possible. A solid chain of pawns on light squares also shuts in the c8-bishop.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Nd7.strategy: Supports …e5 and …c5 but shuts in the c8-bishop, and on d7 the knight can be pinned to the king by Bb5. White develops freely while Black still has to free the bishop.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does nothing for the centre. Bxa6 bxa6 saddles Black with doubled a-pawns, and the knight would stand better on a central square.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Bd7.strategy: Puts the bishop on a passive square, where it does nothing for the centre and takes d7 from the b8-knight. The bishop has no target there, and White develops freely.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Be6.strategy: Puts the bishop in front of the e-pawn, which blocks it completely, so the f8-bishop stays shut in until the e6-bishop moves again or a kingside pawn move frees it. The bishop does less on e6 than on f5, and Nf3-g5 can hit it with tempo.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Qd7.strategy: Puts the queen on d7, where it shuts in the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the b8-knight. White develops freely and can gain time with Ne5 against the queen.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Qd6.strategy: Takes the queen out early onto the a3–f8 diagonal, where Ba3 attacks it at once, so it must move again or be shielded by …c5. No minor piece is developed, and the queen keeps losing time while White builds up freely.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim on its way to f5, instead of on f6, where it would control e4 and d5. On h6 it controls no central square, and White develops freely.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 a6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn without developing a piece or touching the centre. It takes b5 from the f1-bishop and prepares …b5, but White simply develops.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 a5.strategy: Gains space on the queenside and prepares …a4 against the b3-pawn, but develops nothing and does not touch the centre. White simply develops, or stops the pawn with a4.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 f6.strategy: Prepares …e5 but takes f6 from the g8-knight and weakens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal, without developing a piece. White develops freely, while the g8-knight is left with h6 or, after …e5, e7.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a prophylactic pawn move against a knight jump to g5 that nobody threatens, while White develops freely and Black's development has not started.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 h5.strategy: Starts a flank advance without developing a piece; the pawn guards g4 for a later …Bg4 but weakens g5. White simply develops while Black has no pieces behind the advance.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 d4.strategy: Grabs space, but 3.exd4 Qxd4 4.Bb2 attacks the queen at once, so White develops with tempo and Black has opened the centre for nothing.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Bg4.strategy: Hangs the bishop to Qxg4. The e-pawn has left e2, so the queen sees g4, and nothing of Black's defends the bishop; Black gets no compensation for the piece.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop for nothing to gxh3 or Nxh3, since nothing of Black's can recapture on h3.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 Kd7.strategy: Forfeits castling and walks the king onto the d-file, where Bb5+ gives check at once. The king stays in the centre and the h8-rook is shut in.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 b5.strategy: Hangs the pawn, because nothing defends b5 and Bxb5+ wins it with check. Once Black blocks the check, White is a clean pawn up with the better development.

1.b3 d5 2.e3 g5.strategy: Opens the long diagonal to the h8-rook, which 3.Bb2 attacks at once. Blocking with …f6 allows Qh5+ and costs the right to castle, and blocking with …Nf6 allows Bxf6 exf6, with doubled f-pawns.

1.b3 d5 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and takes control of e4, so White cannot easily claim the centre with an e-pawn push. The knight also guards d5 from the side. Black keeps the d5 pawn in the middle, commits nothing else and chooses a set-up once White has shown where the bishop goes.
